stem: In figure 3.73, seg PS is a tangent segment. Line PR is a secant. If PQ = 3.6, QR = 6.4, find PS.
solution:
\(PS^2 = PQ \times PR\) .... tangent secant segments theorem

\(= PQ \times (PQ + QR)\)

\(= 3.6 \times [3.6 + 6.4]\)

\(= 3.6 \times 10\)

\(= 36\)

\(\therefore PS = 6\)

stem: In figure 3.74, chord MN and chord RS intersect each other at point P. If PR = 6, PS = 4, MN = 11 find PN.
solution:
By theorem on interesecting chords,

\(PN \times PM = PR \times PS\)... (I)

let \(PN = x\). \(\therefore PM = 11 - x\)

substituting the values in (I),

\(x(11 - x) = 6 \times 4\)

\(\therefore 11x - x^2 - 24 = 0\)

\(\therefore x^2 - 11x + 24 = 0\)

\(\therefore (x - 3)(x - 8) = 0\)

\(\therefore x - 3 = 0\) or \(x - 8 = 0\)

\(\therefore x = 3\) or \(x = 8\)

\(\therefore PN = 3\) or \(PN = 8\)
note: The book prints "interesecting" — a misprint for 'intersecting'. Transcribed as printed.

stem: In figure 3.75, two circles intersect each other in points X and Y. Tangents drawn from a point M on line XY touch the circles at P and Q. Prove that, seg PM \(\cong\) seg QM.
solution:
The book prints this proof with blanks for the student to fill; the blanks are completed here.

Line MX is a common secant of the two circles.

\(\therefore PM^2 = MY \times MX\) ..... (I)

Similarly \(QM^2 = MY \times MX\), tangent secant segment theorem ......(II)

\(\therefore\) From (I) and (II) \(PM^2 = QM^2\)

\(\therefore PM = QM\)

seg PM \(\cong\) seg QM
note: Printed as a fill-in-the-blanks proof ("Line MX is a common ........ of the two circles", "Similarly ....... = ....... x ....... ", "From (I) and (II) ...... = QM^2"). The blanks are filled so the stored model answer is a whole proof; every other line is the book's own.

stem: In figure 3.76, seg PQ is a diameter of a circle with centre O. R is any point on the circle. seg RS \(\perp\) seg PQ. Prove that, SR is the geometric mean of PS and SQ. [That is, \(SR^2 = PS \times SQ\)]
solution:
The book gives only the four steps of the plan; the proof is written out here following them.

(1) Draw ray RS. It intersects the circle at T.

(2) Show that RS = TS.

seg PQ is a diameter and seg RT \(\perp\) seg PQ at S,

\(\therefore\) seg PQ bisects chord RT ....... the perpendicular drawn from the centre of a circle to its chord bisects the chord

\(\therefore RS = TS\) ..... (I)

(3) Chords RT and PQ intersect each other at S in the interior of the circle,

\(\therefore RS \times ST = PS \times SQ\) ....... theorem of internal division of chords ..... (II)

(4) From (I) and (II),

\(RS \times RS = PS \times SQ\)

\(\therefore SR^2 = PS \times SQ\)

\(\therefore\) SR is the geometric mean of PS and SQ.
note: The book prints "Solution : Write the proof with the help of the following steps" and lists four steps rather than a worked proof. The four steps are the book's own; the derivation under them is supplied so the stored model answer is complete.
